title: Are these not men? (1511)
hook: Antonio de Montesinos preaches on Hispaniola against the colonists' cruelty to Indigenous people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena: a Dominican laywoman in a black cloak, nursing, visiting, writing to the pope. Your line was the mantellata. Who did you visit or call? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

Advent, on the island of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean. A rough church, and in it the leading men of the Spanish colony, the ones who hold Indigenous people as forced laborers in the mines and the fields. They've come for an ordinary Sunday sermon. A Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbs up to preach. His text is from John's Gospel, John the Baptist describing himself. In the Douay-Rheims: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness." Then he tells them who the wilderness is. It's them. Today, the sermon, and the question at the heart of it.
screen: `ADVENT, ON HISPANIOLA.` → `THE COLONY'S LEADING MEN IN THE PEWS.` → `A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: We know this sermon because Bartolomé de las Casas wrote it down in his history of the Indies. As he tells it, Montesinos said that everyone listening was living in mortal sin because of the cruelty and tyranny they used against these innocent people. Then came the questions, which Las Casas records in substance. By what right do you hold these people in such cruel servitude? Why do you work them until they fall sick and die? Then the line our carry comes from: are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Are you not bound to love them as you love yourselves? That last question is Jesus's own command, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Montesinos didn't speak alone. Las Casas says the friars of his house agreed on the sermon together and put their names to it. The colonists were furious. They went to the friars' house and demanded that he take it back the next Sunday. He came back the next Sunday, climbed up again, and preached the same truth, harder. It did not end the cruelty. The sermon set off arguments that reached the Spanish court. And one man in that colony, Las Casas himself, who held laborers too, later gave them up, became a Dominican, and spent his life defending Indigenous people. Friars of the Church named the sin of the Church's own people, out loud, to their faces. Veritas, told when it cost something.
screen: `LAS CASAS WROTE IT DOWN.` · `ARE THESE NOT MEN?` · `TAKE IT BACK. HE PREACHED IT AGAIN.` · `LAS CASAS CHANGED HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `LOVE THEM AS YOU LOVE YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up for dignity, starting in your own mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone in your world who is easy to look past. The person who cleans the office at night. The worker in the back of the kitchen. Someone talked about as a problem, never as a person. Hold their face, or picture one. Let Montesinos's question sit beside it: are these not people, with a soul and a story? Breathe. Then look for one small, real way to speak or act for their dignity this week. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, if you know it. If not, simply keep their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Are these not men? A Dominican's question to colonists who were working Indigenous people to death. This week ran from veritas to the truth told when it cost something. Today's word.
Your line: are these not men. Today, when someone is talked about as less than a person, say one sentence that gives them back their name or their story. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Dominicans remember Antonio de Montesinos's Advent sermon as part of their tradition of preaching for human dignity, and Catholic teaching on the dignity of every person is often taught alongside the story of Montesinos and Bartolomé de las Casas.

original.note: Latin, John 1:23 in the Vulgate: I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, the text of the sermon.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous question, asked in a quiet classroom.
what it means: a friar stood up before colonists and asked whether the people they were working to death were human beings, owed love.
what a scholar hears: we have the sermon through Bartolomé de las Casas's history of the Indies; Las Casas, then a colonist himself, later joined the Dominicans.

notes: Claims rule: the year (1511) stays in the title only; no numbers of deaths or Indigenous population are given. The Indigenous people of Hispaniola were the Taíno; the voice says 'Indigenous people' as the index does. A Keeper may wish to name the Taíno.
The sermon's questions are paraphrased from Las Casas's account, not quoted; the carry phrase follows the index. Confirm the paraphrase.
Confirm: the Dominican community (under Pedro de Córdoba) agreed on and signed the sermon; colonists including the governor Diego Colón protested; Montesinos preached again the following Sunday.
'arguments that reached the Spanish court' refers to the dispute leading to the Laws of Burgos (1512); no date or law named in the voice. Confirm.
Las Casas held an encomienda at the time and later became a Dominican; confirm 'held laborers too'.
Week-end look-back (days 1233–1239) is one line in the word segment.

Editor: removed the claim that the sermon itself changed Las Casas ('it changed Las Casas', 'his own life turned on it'); he dates his own turn to a later reading of Ecclesiasticus, so the voice, fork and trapdoor now only say he later gave up his laborers and became a Dominican.
Vulgate John 1:23 'Ego vox clamantis in deserto' and Douay-Rheims wording of John 1:23 and Matthew 22:39 to confirm.
